1.Entry: Observe before calculating. Physics connects measurable quantities such as length, time, mass and temperature. A bicycle brake converts mechanical energy to thermal energy through friction. A phone speaker converts electrical energy into vibrations. Identify the system, describe what changes, and name one measurement that could test your explanation. Use SI units: metres, seconds and kilograms.
1.Basics: Build a quantitative model. Average speed equals distance/time. A bus travelling 120 m in 10 s has average speed 12 m/s. This does not imply its instantaneous speed was always 12 m/s. Engineers combine measurements with simplifying assumptions, such as negligible air resistance. Record the assumptions and check dimensions: distance/time has units m/s. Apply this method to a lift, a bicycle and a water pump.
1.Intermediate: Check a model against evidence. The kinetic energy of a 2 kg cart at 3 m/s is K = mv²/2 = 9 J. If braking converts all of it to heat, energy remains conserved even though mechanical energy decreases. Real systems can exchange energy with their surroundings. Define that boundary before using conservation. Measurement uncertainty limits precision: a 1% speed uncertainty gives approximately 2% uncertainty in kinetic energy when mass is exact.
1.Pro: Evaluate competing physical models. At speeds much smaller than c, classical mechanics describes a cart well; near c, use relativity. For small v/c, relativistic kinetic energy reduces to mv²/2. For microscopic light–matter interactions, photon energy E = hf is often essential. A 500 nm photon has energy hc/λ ≈ 3.98 × 10^-19 J. Model choice depends on scale and required accuracy, not on one theory being universally applicable.

2.Entry: Distance is total path length; displacement is the vector from initial to final position. Walk 3 m east then 3 m west: distance = 6 m and displacement = 0. Over 6 s your average speed is 1 m/s but average velocity is zero. On a closed running track, returning to the start gives zero displacement without zero distance. Always state the direction of a velocity.
2.Basics: Use v_avg = Δx/Δt and a_avg = Δv/Δt. A car moving east speeds up from 4 to 10 m/s in 3 s: average acceleration is 2 m/s² east. For constant acceleration only, Δx = ut + at²/2; in this case Δx = 4(3) + 2(9)/2 = 21 m. Speedometers show instantaneous speed. Do not apply constant-acceleration formulas to an arbitrary journey.
2.Intermediate: Interpret motion graphs. Slope of position–time is velocity; slope of velocity–time is acceleration; signed area under velocity–time is displacement. If v(t) = 2t - 4 m/s for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 s, the object reverses direction at 2 s. The signed areas cancel, giving zero displacement, while the sum of the two triangular area magnitudes is 8 m distance.
2.Pro: Use calculus for nonuniform motion: v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt. With x(t) = t³ - 6t² + 9t metres, v = 3t² - 12t + 9 and a = 6t - 12. Reversals occur at t = 1 and 3 s, where v changes sign. For 0–4 s, positions at 0, 1, 3, 4 are 0, 4, 0, 4 m: displacement is 4 m but distance is 12 m. Signed quantities and path length answer different questions.

3.Entry: A net force changes velocity. With zero net force, an object remains at rest or moves with constant velocity in an inertial frame. Inertia is resistance to changes in motion and depends on mass. A book resting on a table has gravity downward and a support force upward. These balance on the book. Newton's third-law partners act on different objects and therefore do not cancel on the book's force diagram.
3.Basics: Draw a free-body diagram before using ΣF = ma. A 5 kg trolley pulled horizontally by 20 N against 5 N resistance has net force 15 N and acceleration 3 m/s². Its weight is mg = 49 N for g = 9.8 m/s², balanced by the normal force on a level surface with no vertical acceleration. The applied force alone is not the net force.
3.Intermediate: Resolve forces along useful axes. A block sliding down a slope of angle θ has gravity components mg sinθ downhill and mg cosθ normal to the slope. With kinetic friction coefficient μ, a = g(sinθ - μ cosθ). At θ = 30° and μ = 0.2, a ≈ 3.20 m/s² downhill. Static friction adjusts up to μ_s N; it is not always equal to its maximum.
3.Pro: Apply Newton's laws to a constrained system. Two masses m1 = 2 kg and m2 = 3 kg hang over an ideal massless, frictionless pulley. Taking m2 downward as positive, adding the two force equations gives a = (m2 - m1)g/(m1 + m2) = 1.96 m/s². Tension is m1(g + a) = 23.52 N, not either weight. Real pulley inertia and friction change this model.

4.Entry: Work is energy transferred by a force acting through displacement. For a constant force, W = Fd cosθ. Carrying a bag horizontally at constant height involves zero work on it by the upward support force, because force and displacement are perpendicular. Kinetic energy describes motion; gravitational potential energy near Earth changes by mgΔh. Power measures the rate of energy transfer, in watts.
4.Basics: Use K = mv²/2, ΔU = mgΔh and average power P = W/Δt. Lifting a 2 kg object by 3 m at constant speed increases its gravitational potential energy by 58.8 J. In 2 s, the average mechanical power is 29.4 W. An inefficient motor draws more electrical energy than the useful mechanical output. Energy efficiency equals useful output/input and is dimensionless.
4.Intermediate: The work–energy theorem uses net work: W_net = ΔK. A 1000 kg car slowing from 20 to 10 m/s loses 150000 J of kinetic energy. If the braking force magnitude is constant at 5000 N, stopping over that speed change takes 30 m. Friction does negative work on the car; the thermal energy increase prevents a loss of total energy. Mechanical energy alone need not be conserved.
4.Pro: For position-dependent force use W = ∫F·dx. A spring obeying F = -kx stores U = kx²/2. Compressing a 200 N/m spring by 0.10 m stores 1 J. Released into a frictionless 0.5 kg cart, it gives speed sqrt(2U/m) = 2 m/s. In general conservative forces satisfy F_x = -dU/dx. Equilibrium requires dU/dx = 0, and a local minimum of U indicates stable equilibrium.

5.Entry: Momentum is p = mv and has direction. A 2 kg ball at 3 m/s east has momentum 6 kg m/s east. Impulse changes momentum: J = Δp. Airbags increase stopping time for a given momentum change, reducing average force. Momentum is conserved for a system when its net external impulse is negligible, even when the colliding objects exert large forces on each other.
5.Basics: In a sticking collision, conserve total momentum, not kinetic energy. A 2 kg cart at 3 m/s hits and sticks to a stationary 1 kg cart. Their final velocity is (2×3)/(2+1) = 2 m/s. Initial kinetic energy is 9 J and final kinetic energy is 6 J. The remaining 3 J becomes deformation, sound and thermal energy. Total energy is still conserved.
5.Intermediate: Use impulse–momentum to connect forces to collision time. A 0.15 kg ball changes velocity from +20 to -10 m/s in 0.01 s. Δp = 0.15(-10 - 20) = -4.5 kg m/s, so its average net force is -450 N. The negative sign gives direction. A force–time graph's signed area equals impulse. The peak force can exceed the average force substantially.
5.Pro: For a one-dimensional elastic collision, conserve both momentum and kinetic energy. A moving mass m1 = 2 kg at u1 = 3 m/s strikes a stationary m2 = 1 kg. The ideal elastic formulas give v1 = (m1-m2)u1/(m1+m2) = 1 m/s and v2 = 2m1u1/(m1+m2) = 4 m/s. Momentum is 6 kg m/s and kinetic energy is 9 J before and after. These formulas assume an isolated, head-on, perfectly elastic collision.

6.Entry: A wave transfers energy through a disturbance. Medium particles in a sound wave oscillate locally; they do not travel all the way from the speaker to your ear. Frequency counts cycles per second in hertz, and wavelength is distance between equivalent wave points. Larger frequency generally means higher pitch; amplitude relates to sound intensity. Sound needs a medium, while electromagnetic waves can travel through vacuum.
6.Basics: For a periodic travelling wave, v = fλ. Sound at 340 m/s and 170 Hz has wavelength 2 m and period T = 1/f ≈ 0.00588 s. Frequency is set by the source; when the wave enters another stationary medium, its speed and wavelength may change while frequency stays the same. The speed of sound depends on the medium and its conditions.
6.Intermediate: Superposition adds displacements. Two nearby frequencies of 256 and 260 Hz create beats at |260-256| = 4 Hz. For an ideal string fixed at both ends, standing-wave frequencies are f_n = nv/(2L). With L = 1 m and v = 100 m/s, the fundamental is 50 Hz. Nodes have zero displacement. A standing wave does not transport net energy along the string in the ideal equal-amplitude case.
6.Pro: Write a harmonic wave as y = A sin(kx - ωt + φ), where k = 2π/λ, ω = 2πf and v = ω/k. For A = 0.01 m, k = 4π rad/m and ω = 200π rad/s, λ = 0.5 m, f = 100 Hz and v = 50 m/s. Maximum particle speed Aω ≈ 6.28 m/s differs from the wave speed. In a dispersive medium, group velocity dω/dk can differ from phase velocity ω/k.

7.Entry: Current is the rate of charge flow, I = ΔQ/Δt. Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge, measured in volts. A closed conducting path is required for steady current in a simple circuit. Resistance opposes current. A battery supplies energy; charge is not used up by a bulb. Conventional current direction is opposite to electron drift in a metal.
7.Basics: For an ohmic resistor at constant physical conditions, V = IR. A 6 V battery across 3 Ω drives 2 A, with power P = VI = 12 W. Two 3 Ω resistors in series give 6 Ω; in parallel they give 1.5 Ω. These relations model ideal components; real cells have internal resistance and resistor temperature can change. Never experiment directly with mains electricity.
7.Intermediate: Kirchhoff's junction rule expresses charge conservation; the loop rule expresses energy balance in a lumped circuit. A cell of emf 12 V with internal resistance 1 Ω connected to a 5 Ω load supplies I = 12/(5+1) = 2 A. Its terminal voltage is 10 V, and 4 W is dissipated internally. Terminal voltage equals emf only when current and internal voltage drop are negligible.
7.Pro: An RC circuit has time constant τ = RC. Charging an initially uncharged capacitor from an ideal DC source gives V_C(t) = V0(1-e^(-t/RC)). For R = 10 kΩ and C = 100 μF, τ = 1 s and V_C(1 s) ≈ 0.632V0. Stored energy is CV²/2. With a 5 V final voltage, energy is 0.00125 J. The exponential model assumes ideal linear components and a constant source.

8.Entry: Magnetic field lines show field direction; outside a bar magnet they run from north to south. A compass aligns with the local field. Current produces a magnetic field, which explains electromagnets. A motor converts electrical to mechanical energy, while a generator converts mechanical to electrical energy through induction. Magnetic poles do not behave as isolated positive and negative electric charges in ordinary magnets.
8.Basics: A charge moving in a magnetic field feels force magnitude F = |q|vB sinθ. For a 2 μC positive charge moving perpendicular to B = 0.5 T at 1000 m/s, F = 0.001 N. Use the cross product q(v×B) for direction. A straight current-carrying wire has F = ILB sinθ in a uniform field. Parallel motion gives zero magnetic force.
8.Intermediate: Magnetic flux through a planar loop in a uniform field is Φ = BA cosθ, with θ between field and surface normal. Faraday's law gives emf = -N dΦ/dt; Lenz's law fixes the opposing direction. For 100 turns, area 0.01 m² and a perpendicular field changing by 0.2 T in 0.1 s, emf magnitude is 2 V. The mechanical work needed to induce current supplies its electrical energy.
8.Pro: A charge moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field follows circular motion with r = mv/(|q|B) and angular frequency |q|B/m in the nonrelativistic limit. The magnetic force changes direction but does no work because it stays perpendicular to velocity. An ideal long solenoid has B ≈ μ0 nI; with n = 1000 turns/m and I = 2 A, B ≈ 2.51 mT. Edge effects and magnetic materials require a more detailed model.

9.Entry: Light reflects with incidence angle equal to reflection angle, measured from the normal. Refraction bends a ray when its speed changes across an interface at oblique incidence. A lens can redirect rays to form images. A plane mirror produces a virtual image behind the mirror. Distinguish a real image, where rays actually converge, from a virtual image formed by extending rays backward.
9.Basics: Snell's law is n1 sinθ1 = n2 sinθ2. Light passing from air (n≈1) into glass (n=1.5) at 30° to the normal refracts at arcsin(1/3) ≈ 19.5°. Frequency stays constant at the boundary; speed and wavelength change. Refractive index is n = c/v. This ray model works when structures are large compared with the wavelength.
9.Intermediate: For a thin converging lens, use 1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i with real object and real image distances positive. An object 30 cm from a 10 cm focal-length lens forms a real image at 15 cm. Magnification m = -d_i/d_o = -0.5 means inverted and half size. This convention requires negative d_i for a virtual image. State your sign convention before substituting.
9.Pro: Total internal reflection requires light travelling from higher to lower index and incidence greater than θ_c = arcsin(n2/n1). For glass to air with n1 = 1.5, θ_c ≈ 41.8°, enabling optical fibres. Wave optics explains effects beyond ray optics: in the small-angle double-slit limit, fringe spacing Δy ≈ λL/d. With λ = 500 nm, L = 2 m and d = 0.5 mm, Δy = 2 mm. Coherence and geometry determine whether fringes are visible.

10.Entry: Atoms contain a small nucleus and electrons described by quantum states. A photon carries a discrete amount of electromagnetic energy. Atomic emission spectra contain characteristic lines because transitions connect particular energy levels. Nuclear changes differ from chemical changes of electrons. Modern physics supports lasers, solar cells and semiconductor electronics; simple planetary orbits are only a limited visual analogy for electrons.
10.Basics: Photon energy is E = hf = hc/λ. Using h = 6.626×10^-34 J s and c = 3.00×10^8 m/s, a 600 nm photon carries 3.31×10^-19 J ≈ 2.07 eV. Shorter wavelength means larger photon energy. Energy is conserved when an atom emits a photon: the difference in atomic energy levels equals hf. Intensity changes the number of photons, not each photon's energy at fixed frequency.
10.Intermediate: In the photoelectric effect, maximum electron kinetic energy is K_max = hf - φ when hf ≥ φ. If photon energy is 3 eV and work function φ = 2 eV, K_max = 1 eV and the stopping potential magnitude is 1 V. Below threshold, increasing the intensity of ordinary low-intensity monochromatic light does not eject electrons in this model. Above threshold, larger intensity can increase the emitted electron rate.
10.Pro: Radioactive decay follows N(t) = N0 exp(-λt), with half-life T_half = ln2/λ. After three half-lives an ensemble's expected undecayed fraction is 1/8; individual decay times remain probabilistic. A nuclear reaction releasing rest-mass difference Δm = 0.001 u yields energy Δmc² ≈ 0.9315 MeV using 1 u c² ≈ 931.5 MeV. Balance charge, nucleon number and energy before interpreting a proposed nuclear reaction.
